newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: CRIME-WRACKED SOUTH AFRICA GETS IMMIGRATION BOOST.
newsitem.headline: CRIME-WRACKED SOUTH AFRICA GETS IMMIGRATION BOOST.

text.p: The number of foreigners moving to South Africa outnumbered those people leaving the crime-wracked country for the first time in nearly three years, an official report said on Tuesday.

A monthly migration survey from the Central Statistical Service showed that 756 people moved to South Africa in September, replacing 574 who left and making a net gain of 182 people. That is the first rise since November 1993.
But Alida Casteleijn, a senior statistician with the CSS, said that it was too soon to spot any concrete signs of a new positive trend.
"It is too early to tell if it is a trend. We must wait for figures from another two or three months to see if this is a real change," she said.
South Africa has suffered a mini-exodus of mainly white skilled professionals in recent years.

One of the most common reason cited for leaving is a crime wave that has seen car-jackings become everyday occurences and earned Johannesburg a reputation as one of the most violent cities in the world.
Casteleijn said it was impossible to say if the reputation of South Africa's mean streets was now becoming softer.

But South Africa's beleaguered police service has claimed some recent success in its fight against crime as figures announced late last month showed all violent crimes, except rape, were on a downward trend.
The murder rate in the eight months to August fell by 9.6 percent compared to the same period last year with an average 37 people out of every 100,000 being killed
Other crimes on the decline were armed robbery, attempted murder and drug-related crimes.
Casteleijn said the positive September figures did offer some hope for the country. "It would be very good news if this became a positive trend," she said.

But she added that total figures for the first nine months of 1996 were still firmly in negative territory. The year so far has seen 7,811 people quit South Africa, to be replaced by only 4,063 newcomers -- a net loss so far of 3,748.
Casteleijn added that while nearly all those leaving the country were economically active, most of those entering were characterised by family groups with only one or two economically active members.
The number of illegal immigrants entering South Africa, mainly blacks from neighbouring states like Mozambique and Zimbabwe, is also not included in the survey.
The vast amount of these clandestine jobseekers, whose numbers have been estimated as high as 4.1 million, means South Africa's overall population gain from migration is still high.
